utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday you told the Trial Chamber that you had been arrested approximately ten times in Kosovo for illegal possession of weapons. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we were to examine the court files and the criminal records of your arrest and any convictions, what would these records show?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not criminal convictions, but it was just my wish to illegally keep a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said that you were in prison at one point for a year and a half. Why were you imprisoned for a year and a half?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in prison for an illegal possession of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's a long time to be in prison for the illegal possession of a weapon; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not that I did it for a long -- for a continuous period of time. I did it once for ten days, for 15 days, for 20 days, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You said yesterday that your longest period of imprisonment was for a year and a half. My question is: Why were you sent to prison for a year and a half? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you: For illegal arm possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you an article found on the Internet last night. If copies could be distributed and a copy placed on the ELMO, please. This is a note taken from a website called srpska-mreza.com, called "KLA Terror Cleansing," and there is an article here from the AFP news service. It's dated October 9, 1999, but I believe that is incorrect; it should be October 9, 1998. It's titled "Albanian Villagers Arm Themselves Against KLA." The first paragraph reads like this: "Osek Hilja, Yugoslavia, October 9. Many see him as a spy or a traitor but 78-year-old Mushk Jakupi doesn't care. For this aging ethnic Albanian in Kosovo, who started up a village militia loyal to Serbian authorities, it's the separatist Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) that is to blame for the latest problems in the province." So this appears to be an interview, sir, with your father from October 1998. And in the next paragraph, it says: "'When I saw what they were doing, I decided that we would not let the KLA enter our village,' said Jakupi, a cafe owner in this locality near Djakovica in western Kosovo." The next paragraph: "He started up a local self-defence group, with the benediction of Serbian police, that now keeps close watch over this village of 1.600 ethnic Albanians." Lower down, it discusses a sheet of paper ripped out of a notebook, saying, "Either you are with us or we will burn down your houses. Join your brothers." Signed, the Kosovo Liberation Army. But if we could turn to the next page, please, there's something I want to focus on. Middle of the next page, it says this: "But the local regime imposed on the village by Jakupi and his men is not welcomed by everyone. 'I would prefer to have my house burnt down than to live like this' --" this is in the fifth paragraph on the second page -- "said the local representative of the Kosovo Democratic League, the party of Kosovo's moderate ethnic Albanian political leader." Two paragraphs further down, it says: "Between the police here and Jakupi's self-defence group, 'We feel like we are in prison,' said this man of 52 who asked not to be named. He pointed to the local police station on a nearby hilltop, with what he said were about 30 policemen." Two paragraphs further down, it says: "He said he himself had not been able to get to Djakovica for the last four months because police 'mistreated' him each time he tried to get through the checkpoint, then sent him back to his farm."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have a question now, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question is this: Do you think it's possible, sir, that your local security unit at times went a bit too far in imposing control on the people in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local defence has assisted the people. Wherever there was local defence, no damage was incurred to the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify one point. Were you on one occasion imprisoned for 18 months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was, but not for 18 months. Altogether I was, as I said; once for 20 days, once for 15 days, and altogether the sentence term amounted to 18 months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. Saxon, that's how I understood yesterday's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stand corrected. Reading the LiveNote I read something differently last night, but I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday you described an incident in your village where two soldiers came and accosted a woman in the village. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you described how eventually, after the intervention of the MUP, that after two or three days you received information that the soldiers were sentenced in Prizren, one to six years and the other to seven years in gaol; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, the Serb authorities had a strong interest in prosecuting soldiers who committed crimes in Kosovo villages like yours that were collaborating with the Serb regime. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case in the Osek village, I was the one who discovered it with the help of the local police. It was not the police or the army that discovered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question was something different, sir. My question was whether the Serb authorities would have a strong interest in ensuring that soldiers who committed crimes in villages like yours that were collaborating with the Serb government be prosecuted. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of interest the Serb army had. I know only what happened and that the perpetrators were sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you see, if the Serb regime did not prosecute persons who committed crimes in villages like yours that were collaborating with the Serb authorities, then the regime would risk losing that collaboration. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my village is concerned, I may assure you that nobody had need to intervene, because everything was corrected the first time it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday you made some very serious charges against Ambassador William Walker. You referred to an incident where Ambassador Walker came to your home and accused your father of raping two minor females. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you referred to Mr. Walker going to the KLA staff every night between 11.00 and 12.00 p.m. in Glodjane. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can put on the ELMO, please, the next document. The Office of the Prosecutor communicated with William Walker last evening and sent him a copy of your comments yesterday, and what I'm distributing around the courtroom is an e-mail message from Ambassador Walker that I just want to summarise to you, if I may, and get your reaction to it. Ambassador Walker said: "I've read the references to me --" this is in the first paragraph -- "by Muharem Ibraj and can only say that either - he has confused me with someone else, or is making his story up out of whole cloth. None of it relates to anything I was involved in." Is it possible that you may have confused Ambassador Walker with someone else, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know him pretty well, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The next paragraph, Ambassador Walker says that he never wore an American flag patch on his sleeve and that there was no cause for any civilian verifier to wear a badge identifying national origin. "We were there as 'internationals'," he said, "and I felt strongly about not presenting myself as 'an American.'" Is it possible you saw a flag that you took to be an American flag but that was a symbol of something else?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today I don't know what he is saying, but that day he introduced himself by saying that Serbia no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph, Mr. Walker says that the purported conversation with your elderly father, accusing him of rape, never took place "... at least not with me," he said. If such a conversation had taken place, don't you think Ambassador Walker would have recalled it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone knows that an 80-year-old man is not capable of taking care of his own wife let alone pester some minors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Ambassador Walker also tells us that: "The claim that I visited the KLA staff in a village called Glodjane, every night between 11 and 12 p.m. is also a fabrication. I was seldom out of Pristina after dark, and never had a meeting with anyone between 11 and 12 p.m. My meetings with KLA representatives were few and far between, 3 or 4 to arrange the KLA's release of two Serb journalists and an exchange of the two sides' captured soldiers. Both of these activities were at the specific request of Milosevic. I had 2-3 other encounters with KLA regional commanders to try to hold the shaky truce together. I repeat, I had no late-night meetings anywhere, with anyone of the KLA." The truth is, sir, the story you've told about your interactions and observations of William Walker are a tissue of lies. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not lies. They are truths.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: "In a word," says Ambassador Walker, "his testimony -" your testimony, sir - "is ludicrous in the extreme..." Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be ludicrous for him because it doesn't suit him, because I'm telling the truth as to what happened that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yesterday you were describing the events in the city of Djakovica after the 24th of March, 1999, and you described how the bazaar, the old bazaar in Djakovica was bombed by NATO. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like place a copy of Exhibit 88, tab 18, on the ELMO, please. This is a part of an expert report, sir, presented by a man called Andras Riedlmayer, and this particular section describes his visit to Gjakove. If we can close in a little bit more so we can read the words under the word "Damage." We need to read the paragraphs under the word "Damage." And this is Dr. Riedlmayer's description of what he saw when he visited the old bazaar after the war in 1999 in Djakovica. "Nearly all the shops in the historic market burned out, in a wide area covering several city blocks surrounding the Hadum Mosque. "Destruction covers the entirety of historic bazaar area designated for protection ..." And then at the end of that second paragraph: "Building interiors burned out to rooflines." And then in the third paragraph it says: "Roofs collapsed, dividing walls between shops mostly intact, in many cases with the original roof tiles still lined up along tops of walls undisturbed. No signs of the blast damage that would have been expected if the bazaar had really been hit by airstrikes." Would you agree, sir, that Dr. Riedlmayer's report indicates that the old bazaar in Gjakove was deliberately burned rather than bombed? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. The old bazaar was bombed. The small - excuse me - bazaar, the police station, and the fruit juice factory, they were the facilities that were bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Turning to the events in the neighbourhood of Qerim in Gjakove. Yesterday you told us that none of the houses in the Qerim neighbourhood were destroyed or razed to the ground. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a photograph, if I can. If this could be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. placed on the ELMO, please. Sir, do you recognise this man? His name is Behar Haxhiavdija. He's from Gjakove.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know anything about his character, his ability to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You see, Behar Haxhiavdija --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is a witness, Your Honours, who testified on the 2nd of September, 2002. His -- you can find his testimony at page 9314 of the transcript. His statement was Exhibit 303.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Haxhiavdija was a resident of Gjakove who took shelter in a house, the house of his Kosovo Albanian brother-in-law, at 157 Milos Gilic Street, in early April 1999. And the witness testified as well, in addition to his father, that his wife, his children, and other members of his family were killed by Serb forces and the houses where they had taken shelter on Milos Gilic Street burned to the ground. Do you have any reason to believe why this person would not be telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, there may have been houses burned and damaged but not during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's not the --

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Qerim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to suggest why this person and his father, Ismet Haxhiavdija, another man by the name of Hani Hoxha, would come into this courtroom, take the oath that you took, sit where you're sitting, and lie about the events in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There is no way how I can know. I haven't heard anything about that. And I don't know what interest he has had in testifying here. Probably what has -- what he has said has happened, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, your village, the village of Osek Hilja, was never attacked by Serb forces during 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: After the 24th of March, 1999, Serb police and army initiated an operation to cleanse Djakovo of the Kosovo Albanian population. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The residents of so-called loyal villages like Osek Hilja, the villages where people like yourselves were collaborating with the Serb authorities, were allowed to remain in Kosovo. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you and members of the so-called local security unit were part of this criminal plan and took an active role in it. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Any re-examination, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibraj, last night I saw on TV Belgrade that you had stated here that the state in Kosovo used to arrest people involved in politics. Did you say anything of the kind in fact?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that the state never arrest anyone for political motives, only for illegal arms possessions, for murders, for thefts, and so on. But I've never heard of the state service arresting anyone for political motives. The Albanian flag was used in Kosovo. The Albanian language was used as well in schools until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. We can probably ascribe that to some errors in the interpretation. But after that, a term was used here -- I don't know Albanian, but you know Serbian and I will ask for your assistance. You were asked who was involved in politics, and the interpretation came through that those who were authorised to do so were involved in politics. Did you use that term "authorised"? The people who were politically active were those who were authorised to be?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone who was involved in politics was an authorised person in the eyes of the Serb state. Second, it may be a misunderstanding ensuing from interpretation. I already said that when I was a member of the LDK and I wanted to vote, when I returned home I ran across the police patrol, and they didn't say anything to me, but the translation was that I found a tin of petrol in front of my home. I don't know what connection there is between a police patrol and a petrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did I understand correctly when you said that anyone who was involved in politics was an authorised person, you meant that anybody could be politically active if they wanted to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Ibrahim Rugova was the chairman of the Democratic League of Kosovo, and we others were members until the end of the war, but nobody harassed us for being members of that party. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I think we've clarified this sufficiently. Mr. Saxon produced to you your own statement in the English language, and you confirmed that it bore your signature. Do you remember that from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, do you know English?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you signed a statement in the English language, which you do not know. Were you given to read your statement in your own mother tongue, Albanian?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an interpreter there. I don't know him. He read the statement to me, he translated it to me, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, quite by chance yesterday, because I couldn't even know these facts when I was quoting passages from your statement that I received yesterday -- the pages are not numbered but it should be the fourth page, including the cover page -- I read out to you something from the statement. I will quote: "[In English] When my son Kujtim Ibraj was taken away by the UCK, he was together with Isa Ibraj and a person with name Ram Ademaj. Ademaj was released one day later while my son Kujtim and Isa Ibraj are still missing." [Interpretation] When I read this out to you, you said this was incorrect because Ram Ademaj is in fact the person who abducted your son. He was not abducted together with him, he was the one who abducted your son. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Ram Ademaj came around with 20 KLA members, and he arrested my son and my brother, but he himself was not arrested. It was he who arrested my son and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. If the interpreter had read this to you, would you have signed the statement as it was or would you have made the correction that you made yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have improved it, of course. I would have corrected it, because it was not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Saxon said here that the statement had been read back to you, that you had confirmed it and signed it. Could that be taken as your confirmation of the veracity of what is written, or not, based on what we have just seen?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interpreter read it out to me. Whatever I understood, I understood. But I signed it just the same even if I didn't understand some parts of it, because we were there for some six hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ibraj. That would be enough about the contents of your statement. Now, there is another area that is unclear concerning how you were elected. Let us try to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't believe that the issue of "how Mr. Ibraj was elected" came up during my cross-examination of the witness, Your Honour, so it would not be food for redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you asked some questions during your cross-examination. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't believe I did, Your Honour, but I'm willing to be corrected one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, can you direct us to the part of the cross-examination where that arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not you, but I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. No problem whatsoever. Mr. Saxon mentioned it just a moment ago, speaking of some web page that he downloaded last night concerning the fact that people did not accept the local security, that they were against local security. I'm just trying to verify this. That is the reference, and I'm asking, following up on that, how he was elected or selected and whether this can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I'm asking again: Who elected you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday as well the Osek Hilja village has 168 households. Approximately it has about 1.700 inhabitants. If the village of Osek didn't elect me, someone would have come up and expressed his opposition against my election, but during the war nobody said anything, and six years have passed since that time and again nobody has said anything now that they are free. They don't have any Serb militia or police or army there, so they can say what they want, and they haven't done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this question was a bit distorted. Yesterday he said he was appointed by the president of the municipality, not elected by the people. Could you clarify that question, Mr. Ibraj. You were appointed by Mr. Stanojevic, not by the people in Osek Hilja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say I was appointed by the commune chairman. He called us, we had a meeting with him, and they brought the decision. Every village had a representative in that meeting. So the villagers held meetings in every village and elected the local defence members. This is what I said yesterday. I'm saying today too. Osek Hilja village elected me and Mihil Abazi. Every village elected their own members of the defence force. The commune chairman only signed the decision. And this is what I said yesterday and I'm telling again today. And I'm repeating: If the village didn't elect me, there would have been someone who opposed that decision and said that I was not elected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you went to see the president of the municipality on behalf of the village that elected you, and then the president of the municipality invited the elected representatives of villages. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, and then he signed the decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then the president of the municipality adopted decisions appointing you as local security members so that you can obtain uniforms, weapons, and all the rest that you needed. Was that the essence of the role of the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In this article taken from a web page quoted by Mr. Saxon, he quoted certain passages, and I will quote from page 2, paragraph 3. It says: "His militia--" I don't know why they're putting "militia" under quotation marks -- "numbers about 20 men ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there are many websites, web pages referred to by Mr. Saxon. Could you identify the document first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the last one that Mr. Saxon said he'd found last night. It says "srpska-mreza/sirius/KLA-Terror- Cleansing," et cetera. "[In English] Not all villages go along with the KLA's armed struggle for independence, and Albanians who resist KLA may be Muslim, Catholic and Orthodox Christians." [Interpretation] So that was found on the Internet. And then there is another reference on page 1, at the beginning. "Osek Hilja." There is a reference to the 78-year-old Mushk Jakupi. That is the father of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we have it, so you proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 2 it says: "[In English] His 'militia' numbers about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 20 men, two of whom wore police uniforms. Recently, Jakupi said, they seized weapons that had been supplied by the KLA rebels from the homes of Osek Hilja villagers." [Interpretation] And now he quotes -- he quotes your father. I'm reading it out: "[In English] 'We forced them to leave the village. But no one was killed. No home was burned. Not even a chicken was hurt,' he said." [Interpretation] So was the point of your activity to avoid all violence in the village, not to allow the KLA to enter the village so the army and the police would have no need to come?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That was a very leading question, Your Honour, "Was the point of your activity..." et cetera. Perhaps the question can be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you will have to reformulate that question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Ibraj, is it the case that from the moment you were elected by the villagers to lead the security of your village until the end of the war there were any casualties in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I told you yesterday. I informed you about the two instances, that with the army and that -- that was -- that involved myself. But that -- those two were the two instances. Otherwise, we didn't have anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have explained that already. But did you indeed, as it says in these various excerpts that we looked at yesterday, maltreat your villagers, beat them, rape them? Did anything of that kind happen in the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the Prosecutor read out to me yesterday and today, they have to do with people whom I don't know. If I had done any of the accusations he asked me, then there would have been someone in the village who would have told me, because as I said, there are about 1.700 inhabitants. And nobody has ever said or accused me of maltreatment or doing any harm to them other than assisting them and ensuring that the school was functioning during all the time of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So even the school operated throughout the war in your village.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during all the time of the war, the school was functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, with regard to what Mr. Saxon produced here yesterday, a number of documents: KCC News, Free Kosova, Regions, Culture, NGO's, Links. Kosova Crisis Center, that is a source that he showed us yesterday, and then he quoted from page 2 about this event that you described in detail in examination-in-chief. However, we read here: "The Albanian, Sylejman Bajrami -" that is a man you mentioned in examination-in-chief and whom you killed in self-defence - it says, "was killed after having his house surrounded by Serbian forces." Did Serbian forces surround Bajrami's house while Bajrami himself was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said yesterday I was there with my members when that occurred. I called the observers to come. After the observers, I called the police to come, and the investigating judge. I called the police to come to have them as witness to what had occurred, and not to use force or anything, because there was no other incident. There was no forces that encircled anything. After that, Sulejman Bajrami has five more brothers. If that were true, what was read out to me yesterday, one of his brothers or one of his children or his wife might have -- might have given a statement. So what was read out is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will not quote to you from other similar accusations presented by Mr. Saxon. Six members of your family were abducted, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those who abducted six members of your family, were they the same people who control the provision of these statements that are being presented here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I don't think during cross-examination I asked the witness about the abduction of members of his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question, Mr. Saxon, seems to relate to the source of the statements that you presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the question begins, "Those who abducted six members of your family," and then it says, "were they..." You have to read the question together. There is a clear connection between both parts of the question, Your Honour, and I did not make any inquiries with the witness regarding the tragic loss of members of his family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will not allow it, Mr. Milosevic. Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, at one point yesterday while answering the questions of Mr. Saxon, the questions that Mr. Saxon presents as evidence of your violent behaviour, you said that those witnesses were false witnesses. Why did you use that term?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not false witnesses, then someone would have come out from the very village where I live and given those statements. But out of jealousy, because in Gjakove municipality the Osek village was the only one that was not touched until the end of the war. Why didn't KLA dare enter our village? In all the villages that the KLA has entered, the village has either been burned, damaged, people have been killed, everything has occurred, but not in Osek village. It was intact. This is the reason why.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in the transcript it says, "They were not false witnesses," whereas the witness said something else. He said, "If they were not false witnesses, then somebody would have come out," and so on. He said had they not been or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We're grateful for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So where do you see the connection? Why would these people be making statements against you? I mean the people that gave these various statements and documents.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They speak against me out of jealousy, because Osek village was the only village that remained intact. And it was myself and some collaborators of mine that assisted and defended the village. I think this is the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj. Mr. Ibraj, can I ask you whether there are other villages that had this close collaboration with the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I know one thing: That when the defence -- local defence was set up, the KLA killed many of its members. And when they killed someone in a village, others didn't dare continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In your geographical area, your village Osek Hilja was the only one that had a close collaboration with the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were also some other villages where there was local defence, but I said that when the KLA killed some members of the local defence forces, people were scared to join the force, and then the KLA took over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, have you any knowledge of the number of people in the wider Djakovica area, where you spent your entire life and the whole war, were killed by the KLA, killed and abducted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is not part -- this cannot have come out of the cross-examination, Your Honour. It cannot be something that needs to be clarified based on the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Mr. Milosevic, move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, you agree, but those who killed this huge number of Albanians are certainly motivated to spread such lies about the witness Ibraj. There is no doubt of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I've ruled it does not arise out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, in one of these documents -- I will not search for it unless I'm forced to, although I believe perhaps I could find where this is, it's a huge pile of paper brought by Mr. Saxon, but somewhere it says that you maltreated citizens when you took them to the police station. Tell us, please, did you have a police station in your local security?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any police station of our own. We had -- we had an office in the municipality building where we held meetings and when we got our salaries. We didn't have any police station. Not only in Osek but in none of the villages there was any police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you did not have a police station to which you could take a citizen to maltreat him there, as it says in these papers here.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not MUP police. We were village police. We were, or otherwise, village security forces. As I said, we had our office in the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just -- just let me see whose statement this is. It was presented by Mr. Saxon yesterday. Domi Durim, who made a statement on the 8th of February, 2000. He says, and this was quoted to you by Mr. Saxon: "On the 27th of March [In English] I was in my courtyard together with my family. The police together with members of Mush Jakupi arrived and they broke into the courtyard by forcing the gate. All of us fled up to Qabrat hill. From there we saw police and Mush Jakupi unit members while they were burning the houses of Afrim Domi and Fatmir Domi." [Interpretation] Please, did this event take place?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day that it's mentioned there, Mushk Jakupi was in hospital, in the hospital of Gjakove. In the last 15 years, he has been suffering from gangrene. And in the last 20 years he has been to Gjakove only three times, just to see the doctor. And these are not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He goes on to say: "One could recognise the members of the Mush Jakupi unit [In English] because they wore plain clothes, and they spoke Albanian." [Interpretation] So was your local security wearing ordinary clothes or were you wearing the uniforms of the local security?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, the defence -- the local defence had a special uniform. It was neither a police or a military uniform. It was a specific uniform pertaining to the local defence. There were two -- an insignia on the arm and on the cap. It was written there only "Local Defence," both in Albanian and in Serbian, and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But in any case, this was a uniform. It was not civilian clothes, as was mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is quite a statement as opposed to a question, Your Honour. "In any case, this was a uniform." He is putting words in the witness's mouth. The witness has said, "We only wore insignia on our arm and on our cap. That's all we wore." And I object to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Reformulate it, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought it was sufficiently clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the local security have uniforms or did they have civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The question has been answered, Your Honour, answered a few minutes ago by the witness. He can't keep repeating the question simply because he doesn't like the answer he receives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Quite so, Mr. Milosevic. Move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. Mr. Ibraj replied that they had uniforms. In this statement here it says they were wearing civilian clothes, the members of his local security, and that they were committing some kind of crimes. That's something completely different. So what is there for me not to like?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this event where these people fled to Cabrat hill, as it says here, and that someone torched the houses of Afrim and Fatmir Domi?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know anything about them, nor do I know those persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this same passage it says: "[In English] On 25 March in Asim Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Vokshi Street I saw MUP going to Mother Teresa Center..." [Interpretation] Where is this centre in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This centre was behind the Pastrik Hotel. If you're talking about the one centre that I'm thinking about. The centre used to distribute aid. They distributed aid during the war, even before the war. The same centre also distributed aid in my village. And it existed until the end of the war. They distributed flour, other food, clothing, soap, oil, and everyone was free to go there and take this aid. And this centre also existed in my village too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What it says here is the following: It says he saw the MUP coming to the Mother Teresa Centre, and it says "(local humanitarian agency)," and then it says that first they looted and then burned down the centre, which comprised three buildings. On the 25th of March, this man says, they first looted - policemen, that is - and then burned the centre, which comprised three buildings.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not true, because -- because the police was not there, and I -- you could have people who could try to help and distribute those aid, for example. This was in the house of Hasan Kupa [phoen] during the war. Because the police did not need our aid, our assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Thank you for testifying. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have just one minor question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. I thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, you said yesterday that your father had been referred to as Mush Jakupi and your local defence members as Jakupi unit, that -- the Muharem Ibraj is totally another person than you. Is that right? I'm sorry, Muharem Jakupi is a different person from you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even yesterday I said that my name is Muharem Ibraj. Muharem Jakupi is a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one calls me Muharem Jakupi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is, Mr. Ibraj, whether Muharem Jakupi was a member of your local defence.

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was a member of the police, of the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where; in Gjakove?

utterances.speaker: MUHAREM IBRAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Gjakove, but I think he has retired a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ibraj, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Call your next witness, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Saban Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like to greet you, Your Honours. Good morning. Good morning, Mister. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please begin, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, would you please introduce yourself and give us some details about where you were born, where you were educated, and where you worked.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I was born in the village of -- in the village of Rivnik in Viti municipality. I completed my elementary school there in the eight-year school. In 1978, then I went to Ferizaj where I completed the elementary school or secondary school, and then I lived in this place for the rest of my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I was born on the 15th of May, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the make-up of your village? I mean its ethnic make-up. Was it a purely Albanian village? Was it a mixed village? What was the composition of the population there?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: My village was a mixed one, 50/50. When I was a little boy in 1975, at the time in 1978 people tried to leave the village and go to Serbia. Some people were paid, some not, but most of them, they did not get any money, but some of them, though they had a kind of a deal, they did not get their money in the end. For the time being, no Serb can be found in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you lived there during your education, it was 50/50, as far as I can understand, Serbs and Albanians in the village. What was the language in which you were taught in school?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I was taught in the Albanian language. Only one subject was taught in Serbian, and 50 per cent of the class was -- were -- was made up of Serbian pupils. And they had the same as us. One, they had two subjects per week which were taught in the Albanian language. We had the same rights with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, in view of the mixed ethnic composition of your village, from your earliest childhood did you socialise with Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We socialised with Serbs until recently. We socialised with them, we went with them to school together; in the mountain, in the fields, everywhere we were together. But as of 1977, nationalism tried to interfere in this in our company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did these problems begin?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: The problems began in 1977 when the first concert, as far as I remember, was held in Ferizaj. They existed even before, since the immigrants came from Albania to Kosovo, and since then, so as to say, problems tried -- tried to interfere in the people's lives, like to go to Albania, how to leave for Albania, how to escape the Serbs, and there were some minor problems. In 1977, these problems really became bigger and these -- the reason was just to get us away from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The transcript says that the problems began in 1977 when the first concert was held in Ferizaj. What did you mean by "concert"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The concert is a kind of a contest, song contest, because they came from Albania as guests, and I was a pupil there at the time. The first concert was held there, and various songs were sung there, how to unite all the Albanian brothers, unite. And I heard the term "nationalism" for the first time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will not go into the entire history of these events. I will ask you something about you personally now. Did you continue to socialise with your Serb neighbours? What were your relations like with members of the Serb ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: The majority of us Albanians socialised with Serbs and worked together with them until the year 1998. The majority. Let's say 80 per cent. And of this percentage, 10 per cent were against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say -- very well. Until 1998. And what happened in 1998? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to talk about myself. In 1991, I cannot remember the date quite well, something occurred to me, happened to me when our leaders issued the order not to talk to the Serbs, not to work with the Serbs, not to have any kind of contact with them. It was spring. It was spring, the time of agricultural work, because I worked there. No one dared to incite, to cause problems between the neighbour -- between neighbours. And it was only during the night that they managed to speak to each other. To me, it happened at my neighbour. He said that I just -- he said, "I can't find workers." And I told my neighbour that I had my good relations with him and I'm the person who has come here and work. "I will come and help you." And when I work -- when I went to work there --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Fazliu, was your neighbour a Serb or an Albanian?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He was a Serb. Explain this, please.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I can even say his name. His name was Dzelatovic, Zarko, and I used to plough the land with him, with his brother, with his father. We used to plough the land all the time in the field. When we returned, as it was getting dark, they -- normally Albanians returned together -- they were about 20 or 30 people, and they offended me there. And then the reason was why I went to him and plough the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why did they insult you?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: This was the reason, because they had received an order from our leaders not to go and work with the Serbs, not even talk to them. We should -- we were ordered not to have any relations with them at all. The next day, in the morning, when I woke up to work in my fields alone with a friend of mine, an Albanian, my father and three -- my father and three -- and three men -- a father and three men went there and beat me up. At that time, I was in an illegal possession of a weapon, and then they stopped me, and one of them who attacked me, and then I wounded him, I shoot at him three times. By this description, I would like to say that this is exactly what happened to me, why I did not listen to what the leaders said. Those leaders, even today they are not having in good post. That is why I was unable to listen to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fazliu. When we return from the break, you will answer Mr. Milosevic's question as to what happened in 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript it says he was attacked by his father. He says "my father --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It was changed to "a father." It was changed to "a father and three men." I saw that. We will take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You were asking the witness about 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, you said that these relations were good until 1998. What happened in 1998?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: In 1998, the KLA started to go to the mountains armed, in bigger numbers. I wanted to explain what befell me, if possible, something that happened to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened to me in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thought you had already done that. Do you have more to say about that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you have to follow the lines of -- the line of questioning set by Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, but I was interrupted, Your Honours. If possible, I would like to continue. If not, then we can continue with something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let Mr. Milosevic continue his questioning in relation to 1998. If necessary, he will guide you back to 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, but I think it makes more sense for you to finish explaining what happened then. Tell us very briefly what it was that you wanted to add to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that nationalism began with my case, and the courts were working for justice, and I was brought before court and tried even though I was not guilty. As a person, I had the right to help whoever I wanted whenever I wanted. However, the court sentenced me. The courts in Kosova followed the rules, and this I can confirm with my own case. This is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Proceed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You started explaining, Mr. Fazliu, the year of 1998, and you said that in that year many members of the KLA went into the mountains. What happened in that year 1998? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: The order to get armed came. They were armed even earlier. The arming in Kosovo began in 1992, and in 1998 in my municipality people started joining in greater numbers and went to the mountains. In my municipality, in the villages of Recak, Belince, Malev, Stimlje, they were all linked or had connection with the Drenica part. I worked as a forest ranger at the time, and I was always in the terrain, in the mountains, because that was the sort of work I was doing, and this is how I got the correct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in your own setting where you worked as a forest keeper, you said that you were in the hills all the time, were there any extremists there, members of the KLA? What's this all about? Were these certain groups or individuals that you came across? Who were they? Who led them? Were any court proceedings instituted against any of them? Could you tell us about that briefly.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. A person who was a friend of mine, Adem Abazi, one of the main figures in the KLA, we were together in school. I know him ever since 1973. He was the leader of the Jezerce group and the group that operated in Recak and Kacanik in Ferizaj municipality. He was sentenced by the court in 1979 and completed four years of prison, a sentence of four years' imprisonment. My brother, half brother, Ekrem Fazliu, was one of them, one of the persons sentenced for attempts to secede Kosova from Serbia and attach it to Albania. The above person that I mentioned was one of the key figures of the KLA. My brother was a member of the KLA Commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you come across all of them? What commission?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I met these persons in the mountains. I saw them in the mountains, in guest rooms, because my work involved this kind of activity, moving in the villages, in the mountains, and they always moved in the mountains. They were not organised in large groups. They operated in groups of three or four, pursuant to their orders. And later these groups became larger, consisting of around 100 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they armed? Did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Of course they were armed. But they didn't have uniforms, all of them. Only the main figures, the commanders, had uniforms. In each group you could find only one or two wearing a uniform while the rest were in civilian clothes, but of course they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was their activity in that year of 1998 that you know of directly?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Their activity began in 1995, and their goal was to kill policemen, to kill persons who refused to abandon their works, persons who do not carry out their orders. This is their task, to kill, to kill innocent people and to realise their goal, as is the case now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said just now that they killed people who refused to stop working. Can you tell us what this was all about?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: There are many examples of this kind, but I will mention the example of Elmi Mahmuti, a friend of mine. He had this problem, and because of this his brother was killed. He killed his brother, and the court sentenced him in 1992. The court was in their hands. In Kosova at that time, 90 per cent of the population were Albanians. 90 per cent were working as clerks right until 1992. And they received the orders for killing policemen from Adem Abazi and his men. Their aim was to kill policemen and to begin a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please explain in a bit more detail what you said, that they killed those people who refused to stop working. Who was it that gave these orders to people to stop working?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Our leaders. The leaders gave these orders. One of the main leaders was Shaqir Shabani. I don't remember the exact year, but in 1969, I think, he was in Albania. Today he lives in France. He is a supporter of Muhamed Zogu and Shaqir Berisha. Correction, Ahmet Zogu and Sali Berisha. He is my uncle, Shaqir Berisha [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Fazliu, who was it that Shaqir Shabani ordered to stop working?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Shaqir Shabani ordered his friends, his deputies. It is well known that they worked as in one army, regular army, but they operated illegally, and they had their own leaders. For example, Hajdin Abazi, Sadik Bala, my brother Ekrem Fazliu, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to file a criminal complaint against any one of these people who were doing illegal things? I don't mean only as a forest-keeper in relation to your very own line of work, forestry, but were you in a position to file criminal complaints against these people, to press criminal charges?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. We Albanians are Muslims, and it is our tradition that everything which is against the law shall be reported. Everyone that is working against the law should be reported. For this reason, for many cases that I had knowledge of, cases of persons who were in possession of automatic rifles or hand grenades or uniforms, I reported these men and they were sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have cases when you reported some Serbs for criminal offences?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. According to our tradition, we do not report only Albanians but also Serbs and others. Whatever is prohibited according to the law, we report it, things that are against the interests of people. There are cases when I reported Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. These criminal offences that you referred to and that you reported concerning which you filed criminal complaints, do they only have to do with the possession of weapons and uniforms or also some crimes that were committed, very specific crimes?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I saw only those who were in possession of weapons, and they were sentenced. Their weapons were seized. But also cases when people got killed but the security was dealing in those issues. I had nothing to do with these cases. My work was to report everything that was against the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. At that time in 1998, did you know where KLA bases were?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. In Kotlina village, Kacanik municipality, in Jezerce village, and in the village of Recak, in Belince just above Recak. It is kind of connected to Recak, this Belince. This is in my municipality. And in the direction of Gnjilane as well, but there was only a small number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. There in your municipality, in those villages that you mentioned, a few of them, what was the approximate number of KLA members?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Up to 100 members in 1998. Until 1999, they operated in smaller groups; 15 members, 30 members. They were getting trained, they were building trenches. This is what I've seen with my own eyes. And in late 1999, their number grew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you say in late 1998 or 1999 in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to very specific matters. What can you say about the situation in Urosevac after the first NATO attacks, after the first NATO attacks starting with the 24th of April? I stand corrected, the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Before the bombing started, a small number of people left Kosova. I'm speaking of my own municipality, Stimlje, Gnjilane, Viti, and the villages in this area. I would say 5 per cent of the population left. However, when the bombing started, out of fear people start to leave in greater numbers. It wasn't difficult only for human beings. It was difficult for animals as well, for everyone who lived in Kosova at that time. I had relatives who worked abroad in Germany and Switzerland who invited me and my family to go there and leave. They invited me even 15 days before the bombing started. They had set up the camps in Albania and Macedonia six months earlier, because I was told personally that if we didn't leave, we would have been killed, all of us, because of the bombing, and that's what happened. Many people were injured because of the NATO bombing, traumatised. Only the youth up to the age of 18 suffered traumas and are not able to continue their lives normally. So after the bombing started, people began to leave Kosova in greater numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, please tell us very precisely and as briefly as possible, what were the reasons why people started leaving Kosovo in great numbers, according to all you know and your entire experience?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, my brother, during the bombing, was with me with his entire family. Their aim was to make the world see that the people were leaving because of the harm that the Serbians were causing, but it was the contrary. They were leaving because of NATO. Only a small number of criminals who were sentenced for weapons, drugs, and so on left because of Serbia, people who left for their own profits. But when the bombing started, people were really stressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us one more thing: From what you know, what was the attitude of KLA leaders regarding whether people should or shouldn't leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: The KLA order was as it follows: Those who do not follow KLA orders will be killed. And this happened. In reality, those persons who did not follow KLA orders -- I will mention here the case of a friend of mine who was taken by the KLA and kept for nine days - however, he was fortunate enough to escape and survive - he himself proved this. We have brought this case before the court in Kosova after the war. Twenty-six persons from Kacanik municipality were -- who were taken during the night and killed, all of them Albanians. Five of them were sentenced in Pristina about four or five months ago. I was in Pristina twice and gave a statement, just like I came here to tell the truth. I was a witness there as well, and I stated the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us come back to this issue. You said the KLA would kill those who disobeyed orders. What were the orders of the KLA addressed to the population at the time?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: The order was to leave Kosova in later stages, to go to Albania, Macedonia, so that the world could see for themselves that the Albanians are leaving because of the harm caused by the Serbs. This was the aim. This was the KLA order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, in what way was this KLA order issued? Did KLA leaders or maybe their followers go from house to house to tell people what the orders were or was it done in some other way? How was this order communicated to Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Every street, every village had a council of its own. They had their own people in these councils, and it also happened that they went to guest rooms and communicated their orders during gatherings. This happened in 1997, 1998. They operated in 1996 as well but in smaller groups, up to three persons, just to convince the people, because we had connections, we had friendship with the Serbs; there was nothing bad between us. To this age of 46, I never had any harm caused by a Serb or by Albanian or by a Turk. There were even Romas. But from them I suffered harm. I will mention an example here. I came here voluntarily to tell the truth, and three days after that my daughter was taken. She is nearly 17 years old. The KLA network is functioning to this date. The main figures, those who became generals, are those who killed people. I will not mention the younger ones or smaller in rank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... she was 17 when she was taken or is she 17 now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She was born in 1989. She is to be 17 soon. I wanted to come to this court here from Kosova straight. And a witness to this is a Greek and an Italian from KFOR, but they didn't write this down. They asked me, "What do you want to say there?" And I said to them, "I want to say the truth." I didn't come here to defend anyone. I just came here to tell the truth, how things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived in The Hague a month ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, direct questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, Mr. Fazliu -- just a second. Mr. Fazliu, I don't remember whether I heard from you where you lived in the municipality of Urosevac. What village was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the village of Softovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, when you decided to come here to testify, as you mentioned a moment ago, your daughter was abducted three days later. Is that what you just said?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was your daughter abducted? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Five months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did they find out about your decision to come here to testify? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. I am sure about 99 per cent. I told my family that I was going to ask to be taken to The Hague to tell the truth. My brother was there, his wife, whose two brothers were members of the KLA, and I think it was because of this wife of my brother that this happened, that they learned about my intent to come to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in retaliation they kidnapped your daughter.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So do you have any knowledge about the whereabouts, the fate of your daughter?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: When I was here, then I heard that my daughter had called my -- her mother, that is my wife, that she is alive, but nothing else as to where she is, only that she's alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Fazliu. Let us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that's the end of that matter, may I ask what action is being taken about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean about my daughter, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I asked Belgrade to enable me to come here to The Hague, this is the reason why my daughter was kidnapped. If I know who has taken her, I have warned, and my family, my wife, has already informed the police and also published an announcement in the newspaper that if I know where my daughter is now and who is the person who has kidnapped her, I would have done short work of that person and would not have asked for any other assistance, because my life is worthless now. If you have children yourself, you understand me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which police have been informed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police that is now there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Kosova, in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm anxious to know where this was reported, which police office, and to whom it was reported.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My wife and my son, because it's not easy for me to go there. I don't go there openly to my home. I'm afraid of the criminals of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where was it reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, let us go back to that specific issue we were discussing. You said KLA leaders had ordered Albanians through that entire network of their sympathisers and representatives to leave Kosovo. Do you know who it was specifically in your area who ordered Albanians to leave?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There was Muhamed Ademi, who used to work as a teacher; Sadik Bala, and many others. If you want me, I can give their names as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were the orders?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: They gave the order to leave Kosova for the world to see what was happening, but nothing happened before NATO bombing. The KLA members removed their own families two, three years ago from Kosova. As to the people in general, I'm talking about 90 per cent of the people, they didn't leave Kosova until the NATO bombing started, despite the order given, because they thought this was not the right order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the conduct of the army and the police in Kosovo? What can you tell us about any problems between the army and the police on one hand and the population, the civilian population, in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I can only say that they have -- the army has protected us. They have even handed out chocolates to the kids. I don't know how best to describe it. I don't know any harm, any trouble to have been caused to us by the army. The army has behaved like any army all over the world. I'm speaking about -- not only about my own village but also about other municipalities; Ferizaj, Gnjilane, Pristina. Normally the army was there to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, be so kind as to tell me something about this paragraph of the indictment, 63(j). It says that: "In the period from the 24th of March until the 14th of April, forces of FRY and Serbia shelled and attacked villages in the Urosevac/Ferizaj municipality, including the following villages: Biba, Muhadzer Prelez, Raka and Staro Selo, killing a number of residents. After the shelling, forces of the FRY and Serbia entered some of the villages, including Papaz and Sojevo, and ordered the residents to leave." Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Only in Prelez village the army has told, in a very polite manner, the people to leave there and go to Ferizaj because of the bombing, where they were sheltered around Softovic village, in order to protect the people. The army has done nothing wrong. I have not seen anything wrong coming from the army, because I have been in Prelez, Miras villages, Fusma [phoen] village. I have gone there to -- to take people with my car and bring them to Ferizaj to make them feel more secure there. So when I was driving my car, I have seen the army and I haven't seen anything wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you know or have you heard about the army ordering people to leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know of any such case of ordering the people to leave. On the contrary, they have given the people food. There have been also film footage and recordings of what happened. I went myself to these villages that I mentioned. The orders were -- the only orders given were those by the KLA. As to the army, the only order that the army gave us was to stay where we were, and that it told us not to be afraid and that the army was there to protect us, and this is what in fact happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are saying now that the only order to leave Kosovo was from the KLA. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. This is true. Only the KLA gave the orders. Even today the order is to purchase the properties of the Serbs, the Turks, the Romas, in order to be clear of them. You can see them -- these everywhere, even in the newspapers. This is not only happening only in Kosova. The purpose is to have it happen also in Macedonia, in Montenegro. This has been the aim since 1985. This is not a recent goal. They have been working for that since -- even my brother has done so since 1997. Hajdin Abazi, Sadik Bali, Xhabir Morina [phoen], all these persons have, and many, many others like them, have been working for this goal. I know them because they have been -- some of them have been my classmates. We have played together. We have stayed together. They came even to me, to talk to me, to convince me as well. How could I train my gun against my neighbour, my brother, when my religion tells me that the first neighbour is your brother and that you shouldn't look at the colour of the face of your neighbour? For this reason, we prevented many things, bad things from happening, and now 80 per cent of -- they have kidnapped my daughter to prevent others like me from coming here and telling the truth. I'm sure that they will go even and get my own sons. I'm certain of that. But nevertheless, I want to come here and tell the truth because God will help me. I don't want the Court or anyone to help me. Only God will. I want to tell the truth because I know that the Tribunal is looking for the truth, and the truth is this, what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fazliu. Just a few more questions because you have explained this thoroughly and precisely.
