We have already heard some witnesses from Urosevac, Mr. Krasniqi from Mirosavlje, Urosevac municipality, who stated on the 4th of April, 1999 he had seen military vehicles stationed near Softovic village, and they were shelling towards Rakovica and Zlatare, killing four people in Zlatare and wounding five. He also stated that Serbian forces shot at people in Pojatiste, whereas on the 7th of April, 1999, he saw houses burning in Sojevo and Kamena Glava and heard later that seven people had been killed. So it is supposed to have happened near Softovic village, your village. Do you know anything about the events that this witness testified about?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Qerim Krasniqi is a member of the KLA. He has testified here for his own profit. It is common knowledge what their personal interests are. There has never been any shelling by the army in our village; only by the NATO. There have been 12 or 13 houses which were shot -- which were shelled by the KLA. Those people who have worked, for example, in SUP. There are living arguments to prove this. Avdi Musa, 35 years old, he has worked in SUP. On the 20 -- on the 12th, when the troops entered Kosova, he was killed only because he has -- he has defended the people, and he has attacked the thieves and the criminals. Qerim Krasniqi is a member of the KLA. Someone by the name of Bajram Plaku [phoen], 70 years old, was a man I knew, and he said that I'm not of an age to go to the army -- to the KLA, and I will stay here and die here, and he was killed. But there was no one else who was killed in Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you clarify one statement there, that you say the KLA were shelling. Did you mean to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They have put mines in those 12, 13 houses in the Ferizaj municipality. They have thought that the owners of these 12, 13 houses served Serbia, and these houses were blown up by the KLA with mines. With dynamite, with explosion. I don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the -- sorry, there was one other comment you made. You talked about the 12th when the troops entered Kosovo. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that just because someone - Avdi Musa - worked for the state security, the KLA killed him. They killed him 100 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I followed that, but what did you mean by the expression when -- sorry. I follow what you are saying, but what do you mean by the expression "when the troops entered Kosovo"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The NATO forces. When I say "forces," I mean the NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying that they entered Kosovo on the 12th of some month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 12th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this elderly man who was killed only because he didn't want to leave his house. He didn't want to leave Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: He had left his home in Pojatiste village. He had gone to his son-in-law, to his daughter's home, and I heard from his daughter that my father wanted to die a hero, and he attacked the police. That was the only case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, now, did you have any personal losses among your family members? Your daughter was abducted. I hope that is not a loss. She was kidnapped. But have you had any other casualties in your family?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: The brother of my wife was killed by the KLA after two months. One of the perpetrators was sentenced to 10 years of gaol by UNMIK. The only reason for that was that he had his kid there and they went and killed him. And a nephew [as interpreted] of mine in Zega village, 90 years old, he said, "I won't leave my home," he was also killed. The KLA killed him. They blamed the Serbs for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no interpretation into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a technical problem?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably, because I'm hearing you in interpretation, but the witness's reply has not been interpreted into Serbian. I'm reading from the transcript. "The brother of my wife was killed by the KLA after two months. One of the perpetrators was sentenced to 10 years of gaol by UNMIK. The only reason for that was that he had his kid -" and then something empty - "there and they went and killed him. And a nephew of mine in Zega village -" again empty - "years old, he said, 'I won't leave my home,' he was also killed. The KLA killed him. They blamed the Serbs for that." That has not been interpreted at all, this entire passage. It's missing from the Serb interpretation, so that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I ask the Court deputy to check into the matter. Well, let us continue now and see whether we have the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Robinson. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, a witness who testified here, his name is Bajram Bucaliu from Staro Selo, Urosevac municipality - that's your municipality - said that on the 2nd of April the Serb army surrounded Staro Selo, on the 3rd April the soldiers searched houses, then they torched houses, and on the 13th of April three villagers were killed, after which the villagers began to leave Urosevac. What can you say about these allegations, what this witness described? Did it really happen?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Bajram -- I know Bajram Bucaliu very well, and we are -- we have friendship, or we are in-laws because the daughter of my cousin is married to a cousin of his. Bajram Bucaliu has always stayed in the -- socialised with the Serbs and the Serbs gave him -- found him a job at the train station, but he is a man with double standards. He is -- he comes from a family that deals in drugs. The -- his in-law, Bajram Bucaliu, has killed someone in 1992 for 36 kilogramme of drugs. He has killed someone in uniform, a traffic policeman, Enver Sola [phoen] is the name, and he has spent his time mostly in Bulgaria and Turkey. And three months ago he was burned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not making accusations, sir. This is the truth. If something is not true, I can say so myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But am I correct in thinking you're referring to a relative of his?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His -- yes, a relative of his. Someone from his family that deal with Bajram Bucaliu and Islamija. I know Bajram very well. I know also his father Islam. I know his brothers because we have married among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your basis for saying he is a man with double standards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because he was with the Serbs until the bombing started, and when NATO troops came, now he came here as a witness and lied here. This is what I base my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of the fact that one of his in-laws is a drug dealer? How does that bear on whether he is a man of double standards or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is a man with double standards because until the time of the bombing by NATO he worked with the Serbs. Now he came here to testify against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was -- what was the point in telling us about his in-law who was a drug dealer? I'm trying to understand the relevance of that. Try to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told this because I was asked what kind of person he is, whether I know Bajram Bucaliu, and I know him very well, and he himself deals with drugs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, if he's a drug dealer, why didn't you tell us that before? Why did you concentrate on his relative's drug dealing? I don't understand the relevance of that. He has now also said the witness is a drug dealer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, may I -- may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Judges, I wanted to explain to you his descent, what family he comes from, because it's important. The chip resembles -- the chip off the old block, we say. Bajram is a tradesman, a criminal who didn't know who entered and left his home, and he has double standards and he has given false statements. And he is telling that I am a criminal and my family is criminals. This is why I'm saying that he is a double-standard man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, what happened to your house in Urosevac? Was it destroyed, was it looted, or is it still intact?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: First it was raided and then it was destroyed. Both my house and the houses of the Serbs, and the houses of many, many others who did not subscribe to KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You mean your house in Softovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I mean the house in Ferizaj, because I lived in Softovic, but in 1991, when I wounded that person, I left -- moved to Ferizaj. From 1992, I've been living in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was your house looted and torched, yours and the houses of all the other people you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: On the 12th. On the 13th and the 14th I left Kosova, of June 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When they came under the auspices of the United Nations protection mission, that's when they set fire to your house?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. Until then, no house was torched, only those that were destroyed by NATO bombing. I don't know what the purpose was for that. I can't say. But the whole village in Babaj, from Relaz [phoen], Prelez, Ulrika [phoen] in Viti municipality, they were destroyed by NATO. When the NATO troops entered, then the houses of the Serbs and the -- of the Albanians that did not obey the orders - of the KLA, that is - were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the area where you lived, were Shaqir Shabani and Shukri Buja active?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Active was Shukri Buja while Shaqir Shabani was outside. He deals with Sali Berisha in Albania, Avdul Bardi [phoen], and so on and so forth, they only conveyed the orders while Shukri Buja was the commander in Nerodimlje. Nerodimlje, which is linked with Jezerc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Hajdin Abazi is?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: As I said earlier, Hajdin Abazi is a friend of mine. We went to school together. He was called Lum Haxhiu, while his real name is Hajdin Abazi. His nom de guerre was Lum Haxhiu. You could see him on the newspapers and on TV with Holbrooke, in the company of Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the person who can be seen with Holbrooke. And where is he now?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: In this moment he is in Belgium. He has two children, a daughter and a son, and his wife. They live in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fazliu. Tell us, did you have any other problems with members of the KLA after the war? You have already told us they abducted your daughter, but can you describe any other problems you may have had.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, I left with my whole family, and later on my children returned from Skopje to the house of my in-law with the last name Mehmeti, who got killed. Faruk Fazliu, my elderly brother, was taken by the KLA, and he was kept by them for six hours. Amongst those who took him was Ramush Bajralija [phoen]. He was a policeman, a former policeman, and he asked him, "Where is your father," referring to me. So they kept him for six hours, interrogated him and cursed his family. So when I heard that my son was taken, because with my wife I always maintained contact through mobile phone, when I heard this I went in the evening, at night-time, illegally, and I went straight to his family house to see him privately. I said to him, "I am alive. You can go on and kill my son, but I want you to know that I am alive." And I returned, left again, and from that time I didn't have any problems until the time now when this with my daughter happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you say earlier that it was the KLA who kidnapped your daughter or did you just say that your daughter was kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for my daughter, I can't say who because I don't know who kidnapped her. There are different groups operating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you misdescribed the evidence in the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the name of your son who was kidnapped, or who was held for six hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Faruk Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He is wrongly described in the transcript as your elderly brother.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he is my older son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, you said that you testified before the UNMIK police in Pristina in connection with large-scale abduction in Kacanik. When did this abduction take place? You mentioned there were 26 people who were abducted. Was this during the bombing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I would simply like to point out to the Chamber that the Rule 65 ter summary provided to the Prosecution for this witness says the following: "Albanian; cooperated with the police in Urosevac; will testify about his cooperation, his knowledge of the events in that area, and the relations with the Serbs." Now the accused is asking him about a completely different municipality, and I would at least ask that the accused be directed to stay within the limits of his 65 ter summary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, why are you raising this question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I'm raising it firstly because it fully fits into what Mr. Saxon quoted awhile ago. The witness is testifying to matters within his personal knowledge. Secondly, this falls within the context of the expulsion of people which this witness testified about. Twenty-six Albanians were abducted during the bombing. One managed to escape. There was a trial in Kosovo in connection with this. Crimes committed by members of the KLA were ascribed to Serbs. The witness knows of this and of course he should testify about it. I see nothing that Mr. Saxon could object to apart from the fact that he doesn't like this witness testifying to something that runs completely counter to what is mentioned in these accusations against me in the indictment. It says in 65 ter here something about cooperation with the authorities. I asked the witness about it. He reported both Serbs and Albanians who committed crimes, and that was what his cooperation with the authorities consisted in. And he was also a forester, so it was his job to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, what is the effect of the 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The effect of the 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The effect of the one-sentence long 65 ter summary, Your Honour, is to provide the Prosecution, or to put -- better said, perhaps, to put the Prosecution on notice of what this witness is going to deal with in his evidence so that the Prosecution can properly prepare to test this witness's evidence during cross-examination, which is all part of the purpose of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where is that? Where is that set out? 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, it's been -- I received it in a confidential witness schedule number 35, Your Honour. I can give you my copy, if you'd like. I can pass it right up to you right now, if you would like, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I'm trying to ascertain the purpose of the 65 ter list. Mr. Kay, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: As I understand, Your Honour, there isn't an explanation within the Rules itself. It's from, I presume, jurisprudence but I can't put my finger on it at the moment. It seems, in my submission, that the summaries are really used as indicative of the testimony and are not necessarily exhaustive. Your Honours will be aware that the testimony that this witness is being asked to give relates to Kacanik, which is in fact the municipality just next door to his, Ferizaj, and it's clear that he has personal knowledge of events which Prosecution has been given notice of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour? The Prosecution has not been given any notice that this witness has personal knowledge of the events in the Kacanik municipality. How, then, can the Prosecution properly and fully deal with this evidence in cross-examination? And what other reason for this Rule to provide these summaries to the other party Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in advance could there be than to provide sufficient notice so that the other party can fully prepare to test this evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But if you are embarrassed, that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not embarrassed. The Prosecution is not embarrassed, Your Honour. We're simply asking -- asking for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't mean embarrassed in a technical sense, meaning that you are taken by surprise, then that could be dealt with in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just add something, because Mr. Saxon hasn't been in court when we've been dealing with this on earlier occasions. You will remember that there's a long history of filings about 65 ter summaries, and right at the beginning, I think, from the jurisprudence you can identify two functions served by the 65 ter summaries; management of the evidence by the Court, and that I think became the principal function judged as relevant by this Chamber although other Chambers have held that the purpose is to give the Prosecution adequate notice to prepare for cross-examination. More recently I think the Court has indeed expressed some concerns about the brevity of the 65 ter summaries, of which we've been complaining for a long period of time, without, in the event, requiring the accused to provide much more detail. However, there did come a time when it amended its practice a few witnesses ago and asked the accused to give an opening statement summarising in rather more detail than was on the 65 ter summary that which the witness was going to give. Nevertheless we've accepted the Chamber's earlier rulings to the effect that these brief 65 ter summaries serve the purpose of Court management and putting the Prosecution on notice, to the extent that the jurisprudence indicates is its function, for cross-examination purposes. I have to say, looking at this particular 65 ter summary and listening to the really quite extreme allegations made against individuals, that the Chamber will have in mind that we're going to be completely incapable of dealing satisfactorily with any of those allegations if they are relevant because we haven't had any notice of them in advance, but that's just one of the problems. But I think that's the history of the 65 ter litigation in bold outline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Our microphone is out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll need to shout at you then, I'm sorry. If you'll excuse me just for raising my voice. Rule 68 allows the Trial Chamber to decide on -- to decide on sanctions to be imposed on a party which fails to perform its disclosure obligations, and that envisages that more than the Prosecutor has disclosure obligations. What other than 65 ter (G), is it, could be described as the disclosure obligation of the accused?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I understand it, the extent of the accused's disclosure obligation in relation to the specific, the giving of notice in the summary, it is confined to that alone, and Your Honours have been concerned to not place an over-onerous burden on the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But all I'm trying to identify is whether there is a power within the Rules for the Trial Chamber to take action if it considers that there's been a failure to comply with a 65 ter obligation. That's a question of interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we certainly haven't taken a strong line on that at any stage so far. But would it be reasonable to construe 68 bis as extending to the obligations in Rule 65 ter?

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may also have the power -- if I may address that in a moment. Your Honour obviously has the power under Rule 54 in the orders that the Trial Chamber can make which gives the Trial Chamber a generic power. The interpretation of Rule 68 bis may be open to that. In my understanding, it has not been used in that way prior to today's hearings and prior to these proceedings. There's no jurisprudence that I am aware of that the interpretation that Your Honour has lent or may lend has existed or does exist in the jurisprudence to this extent now. May I just briefly address one further point in response to Mr. Nice. It is clear, and in our submission evident, that the Prosecution has brought an extensive case in relation to the municipality of Kacanik. If it is the case, and it's not entirely clear to me at the moment, but if it is the case that this witness can give evidence on the movement or the reasons why people were leaving Kacanik, or the motivations as to why people left Kacanik, he should be given the opportunity to do so, given the limited amount of time within the case for presentation of evidence. And if it is in fact the case that the Prosecution needs time to prepare that, then that may be something the Trial Chamber may have to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what I meant when I spoke of embarrassment.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have one question to Mr. Saxon. The summary of this witness says like this: "Albanian; cooperated with the police in Urosevac; will testify about his cooperation, his knowledge of the events in that area." Given that Kacanik is just located nearby Urosevac, will "that area" not include the area of Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, not for the Prosecution, Your Honour. Let me just remind you -- if the accused will let me finish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let Mr. Saxon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon is speaking, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Kwon, I don't mean to make light of your question, but Pristina is also close to Urosevac. One could argue that Istok is also close to Urosevac, as is Stimlje is close to Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The point is -- the point is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Saxon, you didn't object when the witness was dealing with KLA bases located in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: During --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's because, Your Honour, the witness's testimony about that came in response to a general question from the accused about the location of KLA bases, and I didn't know what the response was going to be. And now I think I'm in a different situation here. We're getting -- the question was formulated regarding events in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, even if you are right that the 65 ter is confining - and I don't necessarily agree with that - wouldn't there be a discretion within the Chamber to allow a question like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course there is discretion with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to draw your attention to one fact: Kacanik is not close to Urosevac. Kacanik belongs to the area of the SUP of Urosevac, the SUP that the witness cooperated with. Kacanik is covered by the Urosevac SUP. So it fully belongs to that area. You can look that up in the documents and also in the map pertaining to the organisation of the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, before we adjourn, I'd think I'd like to decide the matter, not necessarily on that strict geographical point you've just raised, because I think it's a question of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will allow the question, but we'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Fazliu, you gave a statement to the UNMIK police in relation to what happened in Kacanik. Tell us: When did this happen, what happened, what did you learn, and who were you in contact with specifically?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I said even earlier that I worked as a forest-keeper and that my duty was to go to various mountains, houses, villages. And it is known that usually in the mountains the spies and the thieves go to those places, and my duty was to protect the forests. I was very fair in my duty. I tried to perform all my duties. This was why I kept a close watch on the terrain from Strpce, Stimlje, to Ferizaj. Normally it is common knowledge that someone who is dressed in uniform can perform his functions all over the territory of the state, and I have seen in many instances such people, because they trusted me at the beginning. They didn't keep away from me. I have seen the automatic rifles. I didn't report them openly. For example, when a police patrol came by, I warned -- I told them that this and this person is here and here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, just concentrate on the question asked by Mr. Milosevic. When did this happen, and with whom were you in contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened in 1993, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And with whom were you in contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With friends, with comrades, co-villagers in the mountains, with KLA people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, what do you know about the kidnapping of these 26 persons that you made a statement about to UNMIK?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I mentioned it even earlier. I will do it again. I didn't give to anyone a statement on what I was going to speak here, only the truth that I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just answer the question. Concentrate on the question asked. I know you have your story to tell, but just listen to the questions asked by Mr. Milosevic, and just answer them as directly as possible. So that question now was: What do you know about the kidnapping of the 26 persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My friend Agim Laniste, who is from Laniste village, Kacanik municipality, a village that is linked with Kacanik, he was kidnapped. He was kept for nine days. When they wanted to send him to Drenica parts through the mountains, he had a clash and, fortunately enough for him, he managed to escape. He came straight to SUP, and SUP informed me about that and asked me if I wanted to meet my friend. So I had to go and see him because I was informed of his case by his brother nine days before he was in SUP. I could see how he was stabbed with different objects, screwdrivers. They had asked him, "Why do you speak with Serbs? Why did you send wood, burning wood, to Serbs?" Because Agim Laniste had no assignments whatsoever. He came then to me because he couldn't go back to his own municipality. This happened before the bombing, a month and a half before the bombings, and he stayed with me and my family in the same room, and then together with him we left for Serbia when the NATO forces entered. He then returned to his home and he stayed there secretly, like in a sort of house arrest. A brother of his who lives abroad in France, he has another brother living in Belgium, told UNMIK that his brother, referring to my friend, is in house arrest and had been previously kidnapped, and if this is a matter to be tried, then bring it before trial. And if it's not going to be tried, then please help him regulate the documentation and get to Belgium. UNMIK then intervened, and they went and fetched Agim. Agim then told where he had been and where he had stayed. He gave a statement to UNMIK authorities. Then they called me and asked me how things happened. I told them how I saw Agim, and Agim then told them about the 26 persons, gave their names and last names because these persons were from his village, they were from the area of Viti, and he knew all of them, so Agim gave a statement, and UNMIK has that statement to this date. Correction: UNMIK is protecting Agim. I then went to Pristina and gave a statement, as I said earlier. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Five of the perpetrators have been sentenced. They -- two of them were from Nerodimlje. I don't know the exact date, but they were sentenced three or four months ago for kidnapping 26 Albanians from their own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, do you know the answer to the following question, why those 26 Albanians were abducted, and when were they abducted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt. There is a technical problem with the Albanian booth, and we'll stop for five minutes. Five minutes. I am advised we can now continue, so Mr. Milosevic, you had asked a question, and Mr. Fazliu --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were all kidnapped a month and a half before the bombing, after the KLA took to the mountains in greater numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you were also asked if you were able to say why they were abducted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were abducted because they worked with the Serbs and did not want to separate from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is anything known about the fate of these people now?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: They have all been killed. Agim has confirmed this as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does anyone know who it was that abducted them? Because Agim fled. I assume that he saw who had abducted them. Are the perpetrators of this kidnapping and killing of these 26 Albanians known?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Of course the authors are known. Five of them, as I said, have been sentenced by UNMIK authorities, and the others fled Kosova and went to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These persons who were tried by the UNMIK authorities, were they members of the KLA and, if so, what unit, what group, and from what village or town did they come?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: They were in Kotlina village. I don't know the number of the brigade they belonged to. I don't know exactly the number of the brigade, but I know that they were in Kotlina. And I'm only saying things that I know 100 per cent. They were from a brigade that operated in Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Fazliu. Just a few more questions. The village of Racak is in your area too. Did you see members of the KLA at any time in the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Of course I did, because Islam Belince was taken by the Racak army only for having worked in a school, and the forest rangers were stop by in his house and have a rest, and the police kidnapped him just because he welcomed the forest rangers in his house. But his son, who was also kidnapped, was released, and he is a witness to this. He is still alive. I had a friend, Xhim Koshari [phoen], Xhim Idrizi [phoen], and Fadil Idrizi was one of the commanders of the KLA in Racak. He came from abroad, from Switzerland, because he used to work in Switzerland. Ever since 1998, I've known this. He asked for a generator. I asked him, "Why do you need it?" He said, "I need it for my home." And he told me that they were getting ready, getting prepared in the mountains, and I saw with my own eyes that they prepared themselves a year before in Racak village, in Jezerc, and in Kotlina. I know it is true as far as these three places are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milosevic. I didn't follow you when you said Racak is in his area. You also meant that Racak is under the jurisdiction of Urosevac police? Is it true, Mr. Fazliu?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Racak is 13 kilometres far from Ferizaj, and the police was under Ferizaj municipality, because Racak and Stimlje have only one kilometre in between, while Belince and Racak half a kilometre. As a forest ranger I know this because I used to walk on foot through these villages. Racak, Stimlje, and Belince, and Suva Reka municipality are connected to Jezerce. We all share a same forest. You can see this on the map as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, when he said his area, I actually meant Mr. Fazliu's area as a forester. That's the area where he passed as a forester, because the forests in that area are part of his workplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about this, Mr. Fazliu. How many members of the -- of the KLA were in Racak? You said that you saw KLA members in Racak, Jezerce, and Kotlina. How many were in Kotlina, how many in Racak, how many in Jezerce? Approximately, at least.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Approximately the number is above 100. I can't give you the exact figure but there weren't more than that. Around 100, 120, 150. I don't know the exact number, though. But surely they were not under 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I can't see the transcript any longer, that particular part, was this a misinterpretation or something, but, Mr. Robinson, in the transcript it said that the police had kidnapped a man mentioned by Mr. Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you said, Mr. Fazliu, that the police kidnapped someone?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: The KLA. The police does not kidnap people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question, Mr. Fazliu. Your wife and children still live in Urosevac. Do you fear for their safety?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: When I decided to come here, and many of my friends would have done the same, but by doing that they would endanger their families and that's why they cannot come here and tell the truth. And to put it shortly, I believe that the same way they're following my movements they could destroy my family as well. But I have made up my mind. I want the Court to know the truth. I didn't come here to defend anyone. Even then when I gave my statement in Kosova, I asked to come here and provide a testimony. Those there were people from KFOR and UNMIK. They weren't from the streets, those people that I asked to allow me to come here, but they asked me what I wanted to say here before this Court, and I told them that I want to tell the truth, and I didn't give any statement prior to this one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You fear for your own safety as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. I know that I am already dead after I finish my testimony. Because one of my friends, Naser Hajziri, was tied to a tractor and killed. Isuf Sakica as well, and many, many others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that will not be realised and that is a hyperbolic comment. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned that after the NATO bombing campaign began on the 24th of March, 1999 -- can you hear me, sir?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I didn't get a translation. Can you hear me, sir? I'm not getting --

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You mentioned that after the NATO bombing campaign began -- now I'm getting Albanian in my headphones. I'll try again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That after the NATO bombing campaign began, people started leaving Kosovo because they were afraid of the bombing. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And that there was -- because of the bombing, there was a lot of stress; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You and your own family left Kosovo in the middle of June 1999. That's what you testified to; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So I guess you and your family didn't feel a great deal of fear from that NATO bombing, did you?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Of course we felt a great deal of fear, but there was nowhere we could go. Those who left, they didn't live in good conditions. They had to live in the mountains. But their aim was to remove people from their homes so that the world could see that. I said to myself it's better that they kill my own child in my house than in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And on the 14th -- on the 14th of June, 1999, when the Serb forces began to leave Kosovo, you and your family left and went to Macedonia; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: No. I went to Serbia first and then I went to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So there was a place for you and your family to go if you had been afraid of the NATO bombs; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, I had a place where to go. They invited me to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: But I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you and your family, your wife and your nearest and dearest, stayed in Kosovo for the next two and a half months while that bombing was going on; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Many members of our family left because I didn't believe that NATO was going to bomb. I thought it was a propaganda. I didn't think that a human being would bomb another human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you answer my question, sir? Sir, can you answer my question? You and your wife and your children remained in Kosovo for two and a half months after the NATO bombing began; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Not only my family but families in Prelez, Miraz [phoen], Rahovic [phoen], in Ferizaj municipality. Not a single member left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned Bajram Bucaliu, and you made a number of comments and allegations about him, and you mentioned that he worked at the train station in Ferizaj. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall about how many people were employed at that train station in Ferizaj? Must have been a station-master, clerks. Do you recall approximately how many people worked there?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I don't know how many worked there because that wasn't of much interest for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you see, there's an exhibit that's in evidence in this case - it's Exhibit 63, Your Honours - and it's a log of the train traffic made from -- of the train traffic that went through the Ferizaj railroad station between January and June 1999. And if one looks at this log, you can see different handwritings, handwritings of different persons on it. And I'm just wondering whether you have any comments to make about the character or characters of the other persons who worked at the Ferizaj train station and who might have made entries into this logbook.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I don't understand your question very well. In relation to what is your question? What about the train, because the train always moved in the same time, had the same itinerary. So I don't know what kind of answer you want me to give you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you asking him, Mr. Saxon, why he has singled out Bajram --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's not what I'm asking. There may have been a problem in the translation. I'll try to rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: My question is this: Apart from Bajram Bucaliu, do you want to make any allegations about the characters or the personalities of the other persons who worked at the Ferizaj train station? Were they all criminals? Were they all drug dealers? Were they all persons of double standards? If you know. If you don't know, that's fine, you can just say so.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: As for Bajram Bucaliu, I know that he is like that because he is an in-law of mine. And as for others, there are no relatives of mine, and I don't know anything about them because those that I knew, my colleagues, those who were Albanians, they abandoned their jobs in 1991, and the rest were Serbs. I didn't see people here with double standards who gave Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statements. For 15 days my family --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think you've answered the question. I think you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I can give you a longer answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu -- Mr. Fazliu, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two more words, Your Honours. I don't have things in writing. I have them here in my head. I want to tell the truth, and I don't want to be interrupted if possible. For 15 days, my brother, my own children were waiting for a train, to get on a train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, counsel can interrupt you. If he is doing so unfairly, then I will intervene. Proceed, Mr. Saxon. Let Mr. Saxon ask the next question now. It's a question and answer system that we have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You told us -- sir, you told us a little while ago when I first asked you about how many people worked at the train station, you said you weren't interested in that. Why is it, then, that in response to a subsequent question you told the Chamber that the trains always ran at the same times and had the same itinerary? You see the inconsistency [Realtime transcript read in error "I consistency"] there?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, there is a consistency, but I guess you do not understand me correctly, because I stand by the words that I utter always. My in-law, he was the only one who did not abandon his job. The others, Albanians, abandoned their jobs, and that's why I wasn't interested in others. They were all Serbs, and here we are talking about my in-law. Mr. Milosevic asked me if I knew Bajram Bucaliu. If he asked me about another person, I would have answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... cut you off. We've heard your answer. Just a comment in the transcript. At the end of my question in the transcript it says: "You see the I consistency there." That should be: "You see the inconsistency there," just to keep the record straight. Sir, I'm going to move on to a different topic now. You mentioned that in Kosovo, before you left Kosovo, your work was to report everything that was against the law. That was your testimony; right? And that's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you say to report, you were reporting this information to the Serb police; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: The police was joined in the beginning at that time, and it consisted of both Serbs and Albanians. It wasn't purely Serb because it wasn't written on their foreheads who was Serb and who was Albanian. Whoever I came across, these police patrols, I told them. I reported the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Fine. So you reported this information to the police; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you were paid for this information; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: No. I had a salary as a forest ranger from Serbia sume.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You had a salary as a forest ranger, and out of the goodness of your heart and due to the upstanding values that you maintain, you decided that it would be your duty to report things to the police. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I said in the beginning it's our tradition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic has a point. Let's hear him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the question is unfair, because the witness explained that he was a forester, a forest ranger. As a forest ranger, of course that he is duty-bound to report various unlawful actions to the police. What does that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there is no unfairness in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If I can simply note for the record that I think any response to my question has just been ruined by the intervention of the accused, not for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, were you -- who did you report to, sir? Who did you report this information to?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: As I said earlier, to the closest patrol. If I was in Kacanik, that would be the patrol in Kacanik. If the case occurred in Stimlje, then in Stimlje, because I didn't have a designated person to go and work -- I didn't have a designated person to whom to report, because even it's in our Islamic tradition that you should guard your family from evil, from drugs, from anything else that can harm you. And this was not only for the -- my own good or the good of my own family; it was for the good of the entire nation. And my purpose was to defend the people, because the criminals were a minority. They are only 5 per cent. Not all in Kosovo are criminals. Only the 95 remaining percentage of the population are still being harmed by the criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You say it is in your Islamic tradition that you should guard your family from evil and from other things that can harm you. So if you were in the town of Urosevac and you became aware of some unlawful activity, you would go report it to someone at the Urosevac SUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Even now, as soon as I leave this Court, if I see something wrong, I will report it to the police. Despite the fact that I am here in The Hague, if I see someone with a weapon or with drugs, I will use the first opportunity to report this to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's gratifying, sir. What would have happened if you chose not to report such information to the police?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I couldn't have become a criminal. I was not the only person who reported these cases. And as I said earlier, not all are criminals. They are only 5 per cent. They came from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, I'm sorry. Maybe my question wasn't clear. Perhaps this was my fault. Let me try to rephrase my question. My question was: Over time there was an expectation with the police of Urosevac that you would report allegations of criminal conduct to the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: No. The police did not force me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, what would have happened if you had not reported allegations of criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Someone else would report them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What if you were the only person who knew about the criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I really don't understand your question. What do you mean "if you were the only person"? I wasn't the only Muslim person in Kosova. 80 per cent of Kosova are Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the point is, isn't it, sir, that you were expected, you had an obligation to report information about the activities of alleged KLA members to the police; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I've reported that I have -- when I saw the two or three people wearing guns, or -- or wearing uniforms with a KLA insignia, and I knew that they're not bringing something good, and this is a family tradition from my great grandfather that's -- before they were call Balists, and it's like a group go up to the mountain, take women, kidnap them, or -- so I don't know how to explain it in a different way. Of course it is a duty to report it, to report those persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Fazliu, there is a family tradition going back to your great grandfather to obey the law and to report what appeared to be violations of the law. That's your testimony; right? Right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were violations of the law. Those people who deal with drugs and weapons, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you recall when you told us about this incident back in 1991 when you were in illegal possession of a weapon and you were attacked by three men and you wounded one of them. Do you remember you told us that story?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How do you explain the fact that, with all of your moral fibre about obeying the law and reporting infractions of the law and the importance of carrying on with your great grandfather's tradition, you yourself were breaking the law by having an illegal weapon? Can you explain that inconsistency?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes. I was keeping a weapon just to defend myself. And the law itself, it is said in the law that you can keep a weapon to defend yourself. And also, the Muslim religion says that you have to protect, to defend yourself with whatever means. So my -- my -- I was keeping a weapon. I had a permit to keep the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, you see, sir -- you see, sir, but I'm sorry, that wasn't your testimony about an hour or an hour and a half ago. You said, "At the time I was in the illegal possession of a weapon." That's what -- that's what --

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, it was illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you told the Trial Chamber. So -- let me finish my question, sir. It's my job to ask you questions today. So my question is: How is it that when you felt it was in your interests to do something illegal you did so, and yet you felt this great duty and obligation to report the alleged infractions of others? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, I can. We were not allowed to keep pistols. We had rifle weapons, yes. I was keeping this weapon illegally, and I told it to the Court. So the pistol I was in possession of was an illegal one. And even I had -- I was in possession of it even later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, that's not the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Being a forest ranger, I was allowed to keep a weapon, and even this is also stipulated by law. That is the reason for doing so. Nobody gave me any praise for keeping such weapon illegally. I was sentenced for that. I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever enter the Urosevac police station to give information to the officers there during all this time during the 1990s when you were doing your duty?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know whether persons questioned or detained at the Urosevac police station were ever tortured? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, they were not tortured. Because I've reported it, and I can even say it even now. I just saw it, and there was no maltreatment there, because this was an issue that was taken care by the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see. I'd like to show you a photograph or two, sir. If these could be placed on the ELMO. Start with this one. Take a look at this photograph, sir, please.

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is this a photograph taken by Dr. Xheladin --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Shall we establish a foundation? I mean, I know where the evidence arises, and I think I know what's going to happen as I'm quite used to the Prosecution question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, the answer's been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He doesn't know the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, it's so obvious that he can't talk about someone else's medical reports who he doesn't know, and he's a forest ranger, and he's been shown the file from a doctor in the area. It doesn't begin to hang together as appropriate cross-examination of this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- unless a foundation can be established, and perhaps we should do that before we start exhibiting the pictures on the ELMO for whatever publicity there may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe the first -- perhaps the first thing that should have been established was the foundation for the witness's assertion that no torture or maltreatment ever took place in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I took his answer to be a reference to those people that he'd had dealings with, and the question was asked in such an open-ended way by the Prosecutor that the witness concisely kept himself to his own knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please move on, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I will do that. I will retract the photograph, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is the basis, sir, for your statement that there was no torture or mistreatment of persons in the Urosevac police station? Why do you say that? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I'm saying this because at least 200 persons, and I haven't seen other photographs -- if you show the head or the face of a person probably I would have been in a position to recognise him. Just as I am sitting here, I see the faces of people. How could it be possible to recognise a person in such a photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, that's not the question I asked you. You told the Chamber a few minutes ago that there was no torture or mistreatment at the Urosevac police station. My question is: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I know this because -- because 200 members of my family -- I'm not lying to you -- is my uncle, and the brother of my mother, and no one ever touched them. I did not report it to anyone, but I told this to my family members. And I'm not lying to you, because no one tortured them. No one did any harm to them. One of them was tortured, and we can even confirm it even now. So I'm saying what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just trying to understand your testimony. Are you saying that over time, during the 1990s, 200 members of your extended family were either detained or questioned in the Urosevac police station? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: No, I didn't say 200 of them. I said of the 200 members of my family, because you asked me about torture. I don't know of anyone being tortured. This is the first time for me to see such a picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So just to summarise your testimony, your testimony today that no one was ever tortured or mistreated in the Urosevac police station is based upon your conversations with the members of your extended family, about 200 people; correct?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I said 200, but I can guarantee you for 3.000 persons not being beaten. People from Judikarak [phoen], Nik [phoen], Belince, Latiste [phoen], Zega villages. I have people I know, in-laws, in all these villages and I don't know of any of them being tortured or maltreated. I know only of one case of someone having attacked a policeman and he was beaten. During all the time I lived there, I know that only that case happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I have never seen any other -- as to what you showed me here, such picture, I have never seen such picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you know every one who was detained at the Urosevac SUP between 1991 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You know every single person who was detained during those nine years at one time or another for one reason or another at the Urosevac police station. That's your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: They have been detained in the Urosevac Ferizaj police station when they were captured with arms or with other illegal possessions, or -- it was myself sometimes that have called the police when I have intercepted people carrying loads of goods. They were taken to the police station but they were not beaten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You haven't answered the question, which is whether you know every single person who was detained in the nine years from 1991 to 1999. It's either yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said already, of all these persons, none of them, with the exception of a single person who attacked a policeman, the others were not maltreated or tortured. I can't tell anything about other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You don't know all of those people personally, because there's simply too many people to know and you were up in the forest; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I know many people because I covered 12 villages in my area. Recently they have become over 60 villages. I told you earlier from Strpce, to Stimlje, Ferizaj to Gnjilane, that was part of my duty, but I have never seen such tortures that you are telling me of.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going -- I see. Now you cannot guarantee. I'm going to move to another topic now because we need to take a break soon. You mentioned that your daughter was kidnapped recently. Did this event occur in Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, the date when it occurred?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, because I want to kill myself when I heard my daughter was kidnapped, at the moment I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you recall the month when it occurred, when this event occurred?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Some five or six months have passed by. I can't tell you exactly how many --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if we are --

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: -- because I don't feel well ever since.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we're in the middle of August now, 1999 [sic], then your daughter would have been kidnapped sometime in March or April? Is that approximately right? Does that sound right? Or perhaps February or March?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Five month. You can count that. Maybe two, three days more or less, but I know that it's five months since when my daughter was kidnapped. I know that when I was informed of coming here, three days after that my daughter was kidnapped. And when I was here, my daughter called the wife and said that she was alive. My father told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What's your --

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: And I think the reason is myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is your daughter's name, the daughter who was kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Hazbija Fazliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So UNMIK would have a record about this; right?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the hour. Perhaps this would be a time to break for today. I have a few more questions for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you be much longer than another five or ten minutes or -- because perhaps you could try to finish today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think I might be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it from these last questions you're going to investigate this matter before completing your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. I would like the opportunity to, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I assume there's a typo in line 15, page 83: "1999."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. It was my mistake. We're now in August 2005. It's completely my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can the witness just tell us which police station the crime was reported to?

utterances.speaker: SABAN FAZLIU
utterances.text: As I already said, at Ferizaj police station it was reported. You have your telephones, your mobile phones to find out whether what I'm saying is true. I'm here, so you can ascertain everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.
